title: Interval domain analysis
description: The classic abstract domain: each variable holds an interval [low, high] instead of a single value. Operations lift to intervals ([1,2]+[10,20] = [11,22]); if the abstract result can't overflow, the concrete program can't either. Simple, fast, and the foundation every abstract interpreter learns first.
method: Abstract state maps variables to intervals; transfer functions lift operations; join takes hulls; fixpoint iteration with widening terminates.
usage: Use for range and overflow analysis; expect false positives on disjunctive facts (intervals can't say 'x is 1 or 100').

demo.code:
print('x in [1,2], y in [10,20] -> x+y in [11,22]')
print('[11,22] within int range -> no overflow possible: PROVED')

title: Polyhedra domain (Cousot-Halbwachs)
description: The most precise common numeric domain: convex polyhedra capture arbitrary linear relations (2x + 3y ≤ 7). It proves what octagons can't, at higher cost — the precision end of the tradeoff curve, used when the property demands full linear reasoning.
method: Polyhedra as constraint sets; operations via linear programming (double description); widening on constraint sets.
usage: Reserve for small critical kernels where linear relations are essential; expect high cost.

demo.code:
print('tracked: 2x + 3y <= 7')
print('property needs 2x+3y bound -> polyhedra proves it, octagon cannot')

title: Combined domains (reduced product)
description: No single domain does everything: the reduced product runs several domains together, letting each refine the others (intervals tighten octagons, congruences rule out parities). Astrée's power comes from dozens of domains cooperating — combination is where industrial precision comes from.
method: Run domains in parallel; exchange information via reduction operators; iterate to a mutually-consistent fixpoint.
usage: Combine domains matching your property's needs; reductions are the engineering work that makes it pay.

demo.code:
print('intervals: x in [0,10]; congruences: x even')
print('reduced product: x in {0,2,4,6,8,10} -> proves x != 5')

title: Trace partitioning
description: Merging all paths at join points loses precision ('x is 1 or 100' becomes [1,100]). Trace partitioning keeps selected paths separate — partitioning by loop iteration, by branch history, or by value — recovering precision exactly where the property needs it, without paying for it everywhere.
method: Partition the abstract state by a criterion at selected points; analyze partitions separately; merge only where precision isn't needed.
usage: Partition around the property's critical branches; bound the partition count to control cost.

demo.code:
print('without partitioning: x in [1,100] -> cannot prove x != 50')
print('partition x<50 / x>=50: proves property on each -> PROVED')

title: Soundness: no missed bugs
description: Abstract interpretation's contract is soundness: the abstraction over-approximates all concrete behaviors, so 'no alarm' means 'no bug' — guaranteed. False alarms are possible (the abstraction is coarse), but missed bugs are not. That one-sided guarantee is what makes it certifiable.
method: Prove the abstract transfer functions over-approximate concrete semantics (Galois connections); then fixpoint soundness follows by construction.
usage: Trust 'clean' results absolutely; investigate alarms (some are real bugs, some are precision limits).

demo.code:
print('analysis: no alarms')
print('soundness: concrete executions ⊆ abstraction -> NO BUGS of this class, guaranteed')

title: Taint analysis as abstraction
description: Taint tracking is abstract interpretation with a two-point domain: clean vs tainted. User input starts tainted; sanitizers clean it; sinks (SQL, shell) alarm on tainted data. Simple, fast, and the backbone of injection-vulnerability detection in industry SAST tools.
method: Two-point lattice {clean ⊑ tainted}; sources introduce taint; sanitizers lower it; sinks require clean; fixpoint over the program.
usage: Model your sanitizers accurately (the common source of false negatives); cover all sinks.

demo.code:
print('input tainted -> sanitize() -> clean -> SQL sink: OK')
print('input tainted -> SQL sink directly: ALARM (injection risk)')

title: Pointer and alias analysis
description: Abstract interpretation tracks what pointers may point to (points-to sets, shape abstractions): 'p and q never alias' lets the analyzer — and the compiler — reason precisely about memory. Shape domains even summarize linked structures ('this is a null-terminated list'), proving memory safety structurally.
method: Abstract heap as points-to graph; transfer functions update on allocation/assignment; shape predicates summarize structures.
usage: Use for memory-safety proofs and to enable optimizations; keep the heap abstraction as coarse as the property allows.

demo.code:
print('points-to: p -> {objA}, q -> {objB}, disjoint')
print('*p = 1 cannot affect *q -> non-interference PROVED')

title: Astrée industrial analyzer
description: Astrée proved the absence of runtime errors in Airbus flight-control software — 132,000 lines of C, zero false alarms on the target property class. It combines dozens of domains (intervals, octagons, decision trees) with trace partitioning: abstract interpretation at industrial scale, certifying real aircraft.
method: Layer specialized domains; partition traces by control-flow history; iterate to fixpoint; zero-alarm configuration per codebase.
usage: Specialize the domain combination per codebase; achieving zero alarms takes tuning but pays off in certification.

demo.code:
print('Astrée on flight control: 132,000 lines')
print('result: no division by zero, no overflow, no invalid array access — PROVED')
